title: TriGeoBench: A Multimodal Mathematical Geometry Benchmark with Figures and TikZ
authors: Jing Wang, Yitong Yang, Hao Dou, Yaomin Wu, Shuting He, Tingfei Shen
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models show strong vision-language capabilities, yet their geometry-centric reasoning remains insufficiently understood. Existing mathematical benchmarks typically rely on rasterized figures and cover limited geometric knowledge areas and response formats, making it difficult to assess whether models reason over geometric structures or exploit superficial visual patterns. We introduce TriGeoBench, a geometry-centric multimodal benchmark constructed from Chinese middle- and high-school mathematics examinations. TriGeoBench contains 7,000 question-answer pairs and 12,235 geometric figures with TikZ code, spanning plane geometry, solid geometry, analytic geometry, function, and vector geometry across diverse response formats. Each instance forms a {question-answer pair, image, TikZ} triplet: question-answer pairs are stored in LaTeX, images as RGB figures, and TikZ preserves geometric topology, symbolic annotations, and relational structure. We evaluate representative open- and closed-source MLLMs through image-to-TikZ and multimodal reasoning probes. Results reveal persistent fine-grained structure and image-text alignment challenges. Oracle experiments with human-curated reference TikZ suggest that accurate executable representations provide complementary geometric cues; they do not evaluate an end-to-end conversion pipeline. TriGeoBench offers a testbed for structure-aware mathematical reasoning.

infographic.key_insight: TriGeoBench tests whether multimodal AI understands geometric structure rather than relying on superficial visual patterns.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Paired figures and executable TikZ provide a testbed for structure-aware geometry reasoning and diagram-to-code systems.
method: Construct question-answer, image, and TikZ triplets from Chinese middle- and high-school mathematics examinations.
Cover five geometry-related domains with diverse response formats.
Evaluate image-to-TikZ conversion and multimodal reasoning, including oracle tests with human-curated reference TikZ.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 7,000 question-answer pairs and 12,235 figures, evaluations reveal persistent fine-grained structure and image-text alignment challenges; oracle tests suggest reference TikZ supplies complementary geometric cues.
infographic.watch_item: Oracle results use human-curated TikZ and do not establish the performance of an end-to-end image-to-TikZ reasoning pipeline.
infographic.paper_title: TriGeoBench: A Multimodal Mathematical Geometry Benchmark with Figures and TikZ

title: Reinforcement Learning for Global-Local Control of Dynamic Networks with Applications to Systemic Risk
authors: Nils Detering, Florian Grell, Thilo Meyer-Brandis
abstract: We propose a reinforcement learning framework for solving control problems on dynamic networks, where control decisions consist of a combination of graph-level (global) and node-level (local) actions. To exploit the underlying network structure in a policy-gradient algorithm, we introduce a message-passing neural network architecture with separate global and local policy heads. The architecture ensures that the resulting policies satisfy natural permutation symmetries and transparency constraints. Our main theoretical contribution is an analysis of the robustness and regularity properties of the proposed architecture. We derive explicit Lipschitz bounds with respect to both parameter and input perturbations and use these estimates to establish convergence guarantees for a projected policy-gradient algorithm. The resulting constants reveal how architectural choices and graph characteristics influence sensitivity to input perturbations and the convergence behavior of gradient-based optimization methods. As an application, we study the management of systemic risk in financial networks, where a regulator allocates capital interventions across interconnected institutions. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed reinforcement learning architecture outperforms standard architectures based on feedforward neural networks while the learned policies fulfill desirable symmetry and transparency constraints. The algorithm scales to large networks and effectively combines global budget decisions with local allocation policies by exploiting the underlying graph structure.

infographic.key_insight: A message-passing reinforcement learning policy combines global network decisions with local node actions while respecting permutation symmetries and transparency constraints.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports coordinated control of interconnected systems, including capital budgeting and institution-level interventions to manage financial systemic risk.
method: Use a message-passing neural network with separate global and local policy heads.
Derive explicit Lipschitz bounds for input and parameter perturbations.
Use these bounds to establish convergence guarantees for projected policy-gradient optimization.
infographic.evidence_signal: Financial-network experiments report better performance than feedforward-network baselines and scalability to large networks, but the abstract provides no numerical metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Robustness and convergence bounds depend on architectural choices and graph characteristics, so sensitivity should be checked for the target network.
infographic.paper_title: Reinforcement Learning for Global-Local Control of Dynamic Networks with Applications to Systemic Risk

title: ORSMT: Unleashing the Potential of Satisfiability Modulo Theories for Semantic Verification and Repair in LLM-Based Optimization
authors: Rui Zhang, Chenyu Zhou, Jianghao Lin, Yaoxin Wu, Dongdong Ge, Wen Song
abstract: Large language models increasingly automate optimization modeling from natural language problems, producing written mathematics, solver code and a returned report. Verifying one optimization problem across these artifacts requires semantic comparison: unequal models can attain the same objective, equivalent models can use different auxiliary variables, and mutually consistent artifacts can omit the same source requirement. ORSMT provides a typed semantic interface and exact SMT relation queries. It aligns observable decisions, projects auxiliary variables, proves or refutes feasible region and objective relations, localizes refutations to implicated rows or domains and links source texts when available. It then reconstructs one artifact from another, and each adopted candidate passes the required relation checks. Across 3,034 problems and six generator sizes, ORSMT improves the model-code match rate in all 72 benchmark and generator combinations before selection. Protected selection raises the aggregate rate from 43.2% to 88.2% and the share that are both correct and matched from 25.2% to 40.2%. On the 1,905 refuted outputs, certified voting under the shared fallback makes 50.9% of outputs correct and matched, compared with 44.8% for ReLoop and 49.4% for Opt-Verifier. A separate one-round source revision followed by exact reconstruction restores a model-code match for 84.4% of the refuted pairs.

infographic.key_insight: ORSMT uses exact SMT checks to detect and repair semantic mismatches between optimization models and solver code, rather than relying on matching objective values.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It adds a verification layer to LLM-generated optimization workflows by checking feasible regions and objectives before adopting repairs.
method: Align observable decisions through a typed semantic interface and project out auxiliary variables.
Prove or refute feasible-region and objective relations, localizing failures to rows or domains.
Reconstruct one artifact from another and require adopted candidates to pass the specified relation checks.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 3,034 problems and six generator sizes, protected selection raised model-code matching from 43.2% to 88.2%, while the share both correct and matched rose from 25.2% to 40.2%.
infographic.watch_item: Model-code agreement does not establish source correctness: both artifacts can omit the same requirement.
infographic.paper_title: ORSMT: Unleashing the Potential of Satisfiability Modulo Theories for Semantic Verification and Repair in LLM-Based Optimization

title: EPIC: Rethinking Trust Regions for Autoregressive LLM Policies via Exact-KL Prefix Importance-Ratio Clipping
authors: Chengxi Li, Hanlin Wu, Zhicheng Cai, Huan-ang Gao, Wei-Ying Ma, Jingjing Liu
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) based on PPO-style clipping has become an effective approach to improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, standard token-level clipping measures policy change only through the conditional probability of the current token, while the prefix conditioning context is itself generated by the policy. This mismatch becomes especially consequential in long-response and off-policy training. We reformulate autoregressive generation as a finite-horizon Markov decision process and derive its performance-difference identity under behavior-policy sampling. The resulting change of measure identifies the cumulative likelihood ratio of the generated prefix as the exact importance weight for each stepwise policy-improvement term. Starting from the monotonic-improvement principle of trust-region policy optimization, we then construct a prefix-level trust region using the exact reverse-KL coordinate $r-1-\log r$, whose behavior-policy expectation equals the corresponding prefix-distribution KL divergence. This yields EPIC, a PPO-style sequence-clipping method that directly regulates prefix-level policy drift without relying on a local quadratic approximation or expert-routing replay. Experiments on off-policy reinforcement learning with a sparse mixture-of-experts language model show that EPIC consistently outperforms standard and sequence-level clipping baselines across mathematical-reasoning benchmarks, while remaining competitive with routing-replay-based alternatives. Code is available at https://github.com/LiChengxi666/EPIC.

infographic.key_insight: EPIC controls policy drift across generated prefixes rather than individual tokens, addressing a mismatch in PPO-style training for autoregressive LLMs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Prefix-aware clipping offers a trust-region mechanism for long-response and off-policy LLM reinforcement learning without requiring expert-routing replay.
method: Model generation as a finite-horizon MDP and derive prefix likelihood ratios as exact importance weights.
Use the exact reverse-KL coordinate r − 1 − log(r) to measure prefix-level drift.
Build PPO-style sequence clipping around this prefix-level trust region.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent gains over standard and sequence-level clipping baselines on mathematical-reasoning benchmarks using an off-policy-trained sparse mixture-of-experts LLM, with competitive results against routing-replay alternatives.
infographic.watch_item: Cumulative prefix ratios require numerical care for long responses, and the abstract provides no quantitative gains or evidence of generalization beyond the reported setting.
infographic.paper_title: EPIC: Rethinking Trust Regions for Autoregressive LLM Policies via Exact-KL Prefix Importance-Ratio Clipping

title: Minimax Rates for imperfect Physics-Informed Regression
authors: Nathan Doumèche
abstract: Physics-informed machine learning incorporates physical knowledge into data-driven models, often through a partial differential equation (PDE) that the target is assumed to satisfy. However, how much this knowledge improves statistical performance remains unclear, especially when the physical model is imperfect. Since satisfying a PDE implies being differentiable, a natural benchmark for physics-informed regression is the best achievable performance when smoothness is the only prior information about the target function. We show that there is a characteristic threshold for the modeling error above which the physical prior cannot improve the convergence rate. The form of this threshold is common to every linear PDE and certain nonlinear PDEs. Below it, the gain depends on the equation type. For classes of elliptic and hyperbolic PDEs with constant coefficients, we establish convergence rates that improve continuously as the modeling error decreases, and prove their minimax optimality up to logarithmic factors. With exact physics, the rates correspond to learning in dimension d-1 rather than d, reflecting the freedom left by unknown boundary or initial data. We also give conditions for computing the estimator with near-linear complexity and show how to tune its hyperparameters without knowing the modeling error.

infographic.key_insight: Imperfect PDE knowledge improves regression convergence rates only below a modeling-error threshold; with exact physics, the studied PDE classes yield rates corresponding to dimension d−1 rather than d.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results clarify when physical constraints can improve learning beyond smoothness alone and identify conditions for near-linear estimator computation.
method: Compare physics-informed regression against a smoothness-only minimax benchmark.
Derive modeling-error thresholds and rates for constant-coefficient elliptic and hyperbolic PDE classes.
Prove minimax optimality up to logarithmic factors and tune hyperparameters without knowing the modeling error.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical convergence-rate and complexity guarantees, but no empirical datasets or numerical evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: The detailed rate guarantees apply to specific PDE classes, and near-linear computation requires additional conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Minimax Rates for imperfect Physics-Informed Regression

title: Convergence of stochastic gradient descent for learning linear neural networks
authors: Gabin Maxime Nguegnang, Bubacarr Bah, Holger Rauhut, Ulrich Terstiege
abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is the cornerstone of modern deep learning, yet its theoretical convergence properties remain poorly understood in non-convex settings. To address this gap, we study SGD dynamics in deep linear neural networks - simplified models that retain key non-convex characteristics while remaining analytically tractable. Building on recent results for gradient descent, we extend convergence guarantees to SGD under regularized squared loss. We establish almost sure boundedness of SGD iterates. Using the framework of asymptotic pseudotrajectories from stochastic approximation theory, our analysis establishes then, for both deterministic and adaptive step-size choices, convergence of SGD to the set of critical points under mild conditions (without relying on Lipschitz properties or whitened data). To our knowledge, this is the first work providing almost sure convergence guarantees for SGD in deep linear networks, bridging the gap between theoretical optimization and practical stochastic training.

infographic.key_insight: The paper establishes almost sure boundedness of SGD iterates and convergence to the set of critical points for deep linear networks under mild conditions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results strengthen the theoretical basis for stochastic training in non-convex linear network models with deterministic or adaptive step sizes.
method: Analyze SGD for deep linear networks with regularized squared loss.
Establish almost sure boundedness of the iterates.
Use asymptotic pseudotrajectory theory to prove convergence without relying on Lipschitz properties or whitened data.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical convergence guarantees but describes no datasets, experiments, or empirical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Convergence to the set of critical points does not guarantee a global optimum, and the results concern linear rather than nonlinear networks.
infographic.paper_title: Convergence of stochastic gradient descent for learning linear neural networks

title: Adaptive Grid Refinement for Optimal Feedback Control
authors: Alen E. Golpashin, Matthew T. Clark, Bruce A. Conway
abstract: This paper introduces an algorithmic approach for adaptive grid refinement for solving the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) partial differential equation (PDE) to obtain the optimal feedback control. Traditional grid generation methods often face challenges associated with state-space dimensionality, solution regularity, and large variations in the solution. Whereas fixed grid generation methods may fail to capture the intricate details of the optimal solution, our methodology addresses this challenge by dynamically refining the grid used to solve the HJB equation, thereby optimizing computational resource usage while targeting improved solution accuracy. The reinforcement learning (RL)-based approach presented in this study seeks to reduce the node population while constructing a grid with higher node density in regions with large discretization error.

infographic.key_insight: Reinforcement learning guides adaptive grid refinement for the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation, concentrating nodes where discretization error is large to support accurate optimal feedback control.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Adaptive node placement could reduce the computational cost of computing feedback control policies compared with uniformly dense grids.
method: Solve the HJB PDE on a state-space grid.
Use reinforcement learning to guide grid refinement.
Target fewer total nodes while increasing density in high-error regions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes the approach and its objectives but reports no benchmarks, quantitative accuracy gains, or node-count reductions.
infographic.watch_item: Scalability to high-dimensional state spaces and the overhead of learning-driven refinement remain unquantified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Adaptive Grid Refinement for Optimal Feedback Control

title: Group Distributionally Robust Optimization over Decentralized Networks
authors: Haomin Bai, Junyan Sun, Quan Cheng, Yuanyu Wan, Lijun Zhang
abstract: We study group distributionally robust optimization (GDRO) over decentralized networks, where workers collaborate to learn robust models by minimizing the maximum local risk. Existing methods optimize only dual-regularized surrogates and establish guarantees for a globally averaged model that is not available to workers. In this paper, we directly optimize the original GDRO objective and establish guarantees for local models in semi-decentralized (SemiDec) and fully decentralized (Dec) settings. A key difficulty is that applying the primal-dual decomposition from centralized GDRO yields worker-dependent losses whose evaluation requires unavailable cross-worker information. To address this challenge, we develop a novel error decomposition that recasts decentralized GDRO as (i) a decentralized online convex optimization (D-OCO) problem and a prediction-with-expert-advice problem in SemiDec, and as (ii) two coupled D-OCO problems in Dec, with discrepancy terms capturing inconsistencies among local decisions. By isolating consensus errors in analysis, we develop modular frameworks that support different consensus routines. We then establish the \emph{first} per-worker convergence guarantees for optimizing the original GDRO objective over decentralized networks. Instantiations with accelerated gossip and Choco-gossip achieve an $O(\sqrt{(\log m)/T})$ convergence rate over $T$ update rounds, while experiments demonstrate improved worst-worker performance over baselines.

infographic.key_insight: A new error decomposition enables the first per-worker convergence guarantees for the original group distributionally robust optimization objective over decentralized networks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Networked workers can collaboratively minimize worst-worker risk with guarantees for their locally available models, rather than an unavailable global average.
method: Separate optimization errors from consensus discrepancies among local decisions.
Combine decentralized online convex optimization with expert advice in SemiDec, or couple two decentralized online convex optimization problems in Dec.
Instantiate modular consensus frameworks with accelerated gossip or Choco-gossip.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports an O(√(log m/T)) convergence rate over T update rounds and experiments showing improved worst-worker performance over baselines, without specifying datasets or effect sizes.
infographic.watch_item: Practical performance depends on controlling consensus errors; the abstract does not quantify communication costs or sensitivity to network topology.
infographic.paper_title: Group Distributionally Robust Optimization over Decentralized Networks

title: A Model-Free Continuous-Time RL Algorithm from Discrete-Time Off-Policy Data with End-to-End Guarantees
authors: Chaorui Yao, Yuming Paul Zhang, Lin Yang, Yuhua Zhu
abstract: In this paper, we study continuous-time reinforcement learning, where the state follows an unknown stochastic differential equation but only a fixed off-policy batch of discrete-time transitions is available. Standard discrete-time Q-learning becomes problematic as the sampling interval shrinks, because differences between action values vanish. Continuous-time alternatives, such as Deep Advantage Updating and martingale q-learning, preserve the action signal but jointly learn a value function and an action-dependent critic. Building on the PhiBE-Q formulation (arXiv:2606.21925), we develop a model-free PhiBE policy iteration (PhiBE-PI) framework that uses a single state-action critic while preserving the continuous-time action-ranking scale. At each iteration, the framework learns the critic directly from sampled increments and uses it to improve the policy. The same batch is reused throughout, without explicitly estimating the drift or diffusion. We further develop an implementation under linear function approximation and establish a local end-to-end suboptimality guarantee for the learned policy. Our analysis quantifies how errors from time discretization, function approximation, and finite-sample policy evaluation propagate through policy iteration. It accounts for the dependence of successive policies on the reused data, so the guarantee does not require a fresh batch at each iteration. Moreover, we identify a bias-variance trade-off: smaller sampling intervals improve the approximation to the continuous-time problem but can increase statistical error at a fixed sample size. Thus, finer time discretization does not necessarily lead to better policy performance.

infographic.key_insight: PhiBE-PI learns a single state-action critic from discrete-time off-policy data while preserving the action-ranking signal needed for continuous-time control.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports policy improvement from a fixed transition batch without explicitly estimating the system’s drift or diffusion.
method: Learn the critic directly from sampled state increments.
Alternate critic evaluation and policy improvement while reusing the same batch.
Use linear function approximation with a local end-to-end suboptimality guarantee.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical bounds tracking discretization, approximation, and finite-sample errors under data reuse, but provides no empirical results.
infographic.watch_item: Smaller sampling intervals reduce discretization error but can increase statistical error at fixed sample size, so finer sampling need not improve policy performance.
infographic.paper_title: A Model-Free Continuous-Time RL Algorithm from Discrete-Time Off-Policy Data with End-to-End Guarantees

title: Automatic Differentiation with Constraints in Forward and Inverse Problems
authors: Nikolay Yavich, Alexander Ryabov, Viacheslav Naumov, Sayan Ranu, N. M. Anoop Krishnan, Evgeny Burnaev
abstract: Approximate solutions of partial differential equations (PDEs) on unstructured grids can be represented on a graph. Numerical optimization involving stiff evolutionary and static PDEs often requires solving a large system of equations, which can be treated as a constraint. In this work, we present a fully differentiable graph-based implicit solver that incorporates this constraint. We evaluate its performance across four key tasks: a) linear and nonlinear forward modeling of evolutionary and static problems, b) solving inverse problems to estimate equation coefficients, c) solving inverse problems to estimate the right-hand side, and d) learnable graph coarsening to accelerate forward modeling. The stability and differentiability of our solver enable significant reductions in the complexity of forward modeling while efficiently addressing related inverse problems. These capabilities make it a powerful tool for different physics and engineering applications, in particular for geophysics, where inverse problems are commonly solved in order to reduce the model uncertainty.

infographic.key_insight: A fully differentiable graph-based implicit solver treats PDE systems as constraints, supporting stable forward simulation and gradient-based inverse modeling on unstructured grids.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could reduce simulation costs and support parameter or source estimation in engineering applications such as geophysics.
method: Represent discretized PDE solutions on graphs derived from unstructured grids.
Incorporate equation-system constraints into a fully differentiable implicit solver.
Learn graph coarsening to accelerate forward modeling.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports evaluation on linear and nonlinear evolutionary and static PDEs, coefficient estimation, right-hand-side estimation, and learnable graph coarsening, but provides no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Practical scalability and accuracy under learned coarsening require validation; the abstract does not quantify either.
infographic.paper_title: Automatic Differentiation with Constraints in Forward and Inverse Problems

title: OptScientist: Automated Discovery of Optimization Laws
authors: Ma ZhenYao, Yue Liang, Jian-Qiao Zhu
abstract: Many scientific phenomena are best understood as outcomes of underlying optimization problems, yet automated scientific discovery has largely focused on recovering equations that describe observed input-output patterns. We introduce OptScientist, a novel automated framework for discovering compact symbolic optimization laws directly from data. OptScientist comprises (i) a model that infers symbolic optimization problems by first learning to represent data as an optimization problem and then extracting its symbolic form, and (ii) an LLM agentic system embedding the model in a discovery process that integrates theoretical priors from scientific literature, discovers candidate laws, abstracts their underlying mechanisms, and suggests new data to collect. We first evaluate OptScientist on OptFeynman, a novel benchmark of 99 physics-derived optimization problems, where OptScientist recovers ground-truth laws for over 80% of the problems and remains robust to noisy contextual information, while substantially outperforming machine-learning, symbolic, and LLM-based model-discovery baselines. On human risky choice and central-bank monetary policy, OptScientist discovers compact symbolic optimization laws that achieve held-out predictive performance competitive with leading baselines, while using few parameters and substantially fewer tokens than LLM baselines. Overall, OptScientist extends automated scientific discovery to uncovering optimization laws that generate observed phenomena, enabling automated theory building across the physical, biological, behavioral, and social sciences.

infographic.key_insight: OptScientist discovers compact symbolic optimization laws that explain observed behavior as the outcome of an underlying optimization problem.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could help engineers infer interpretable objectives behind observed system behavior rather than fit input-output equations alone.
method: Learn an optimization-based representation of data, then extract its symbolic form.
Use an LLM agent to integrate scientific priors, discover candidate laws, and abstract mechanisms.
Suggest new data to collect for further discovery.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the 99-problem OptFeynman benchmark, OptScientist recovers over 80% of ground-truth laws; on risky choice and monetary policy, it reports competitive held-out prediction with few parameters.
infographic.watch_item: Predictive accuracy alone does not establish that a discovered objective is the true underlying mechanism; independent validation remains important.
infographic.paper_title: OptScientist: Automated Discovery of Optimization Laws

title: Soliton Profiles in 1D: Enhanced Neural-Network Solvers and Constrained Deep Ritz Methods
authors: Chandler Haight, Alex D Rodriguez, Svetlana Roudenko
abstract: We develop and compare enhanced neural-network solvers for one-dimensional ground-state profiles, which are solutions of $$ Q^{\prime\prime}=bQ-γQ^{p},\quad Q>0,\quad p>1, \quad b, γ>0, $$ the stationary profile equation for the nonlinear Schrödinger, generalized Korteweg-de Vries, and nonlinear Klein-Gordon equations. Its explicit sech-type solutions serve as exact reference for error computation and benchmark hyperparameter selection. We improve on the standard Adam-trained physics-informed neural network (PINN) baseline by introducing higher-order optimization via Gauss-Newton/Levenberg-Marquardt and L-BFGS refinements, as well as Fourier-feature PINNs, and constrained Deep Ritz (DR) formulations. In DR approaches we introduce two new neural-network formulations, which implement two classical variational characterizations: a Nehari-constrained Deep Ritz method, in which the height is learned by projecting onto the Nehari/Pokhozhaev manifold, and a Weinstein Deep Ritz method, in which a normalized profile minimizes the Weinstein quotient. The Deep Ritz formulations perform best overall, in particular, the Weinstein variant gives the best error-runtime balance. The neural-network based solvers remain less accurate and efficient than classical Petviashvili iteration in 1D, however, the current study provides a proof of concept: the mesh-free formulation, non-reliance on exact profiles or the related features make them promising in higher dimensions and for more complicated nonlinearities and dispersive operators.

infographic.key_insight: Constrained Deep Ritz solvers perform best among the tested neural approaches for 1D soliton profiles, with the Weinstein variant offering the best error–runtime balance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Mesh-free neural solvers offer a proof of concept for tackling more complex nonlinearities, dispersive operators, and higher-dimensional problems.
method: Enhance Adam-trained PINNs with Gauss–Newton/Levenberg–Marquardt, L-BFGS refinements, and Fourier features.
Learn profile amplitude through a Nehari/Pokhozhaev-constrained Deep Ritz formulation.
Minimize the Weinstein quotient using a normalized neural profile.
infographic.evidence_signal: Explicit sech-type solutions provide exact references for error computation and hyperparameter benchmarking, with classical Petviashvili iteration serving as a comparator.
infographic.watch_item: In 1D, the neural solvers remain less accurate and efficient than Petviashvili iteration; advantages in higher dimensions are not established here.
infographic.paper_title: Soliton Profiles in 1D: Enhanced Neural-Network Solvers and Constrained Deep Ritz Methods

title: Curvature-Scaled Sharpness-Aware Minimization: Convergence Beyond Smoothness
authors: Dimitris Oikonomou, Nicolas Loizou
abstract: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) has established itself as a widely used method for training deep neural networks. Despite its popularity, existing convergence guarantees for SAM-type methods require smoothness, a restrictive assumption. Generalized smoothness conditions have recently been proposed in the analysis of gradient methods but remain underexplored for SAM. To analyze the effect of SAM's perturbation under generalized smoothness, we use relative gradient distortion to quantify how the sharpness-aware direction departs from the original gradient. Under $(L_0,L_1)$-smoothness, we show that this distortion can become unbounded near stationarity for SAM and at large gradients for its unnormalized variant (USAM), with examples where SAM cycles and USAM diverges. We then establish a necessary condition for uniform distortion control among perturbations along the gradient whose nonnegative multipliers depend only on its norm. Motivated by this condition, we propose Curvature-Scaled SAM (CS-SAM), which scales both the perturbation and the descent step by suitable curvature upper bounds, and prove that it uniformly bounds the distortion. Under both $(L_0,L_1)$- and $(H_0,H_1)$-smoothness, we establish deterministic $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$ rates for the best squared gradient norm on nonconvex objectives, last-iterate $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$ rates for the function gap on convex objectives with a minimizer, and linear convergence under the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition. With zero perturbation, our guarantees recover the rates for gradient descent with $(L_0,L_1)$- or $(H_0,H_1)$-based step-sizes. Minibatch experiments on computer vision tasks demonstrate competitive performance for both variants, with the $(H_0,H_1)$ variant achieving the highest mean best-test accuracy in all four settings against tuned SAM and USAM with constant and cosine annealing schedules.

infographic.key_insight: Curvature-Scaled SAM uniformly controls gradient distortion under generalized smoothness, enabling convergence guarantees where standard SAM can cycle and USAM can diverge.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Curvature-aware scaling offers a principled way to adapt sharpness-aware training beyond the restrictive assumption of globally smooth objectives.
method: Measure relative gradient distortion caused by sharpness-aware perturbations.
Scale both the perturbation and descent step using curvature upper bounds.
Prove deterministic O(1/T) stationarity and convex function-gap rates, plus linear convergence under the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition.
infographic.evidence_signal: In minibatch computer vision experiments, the (H0,H1) variant achieved the highest mean best-test accuracy in all four settings against tuned SAM and USAM with constant and cosine schedules.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees are deterministic and rely on suitable curvature upper bounds; the abstract does not establish equivalent minibatch convergence guarantees.
infographic.paper_title: Curvature-Scaled Sharpness-Aware Minimization: Convergence Beyond Smoothness

title: Local Work, Global Progress: A Convergence Theory of AI Agent Collaboration
authors: Ivan Ilin, Peter Richtárik
abstract: Teams of large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly applied to complex tasks, but their collaboration protocols are mostly designed empirically, without convergence guarantees. We formalize collaborative problem solving as block optimization: each agent improves one part of a shared solution, guided by its local objective plus a correction for how its changes affect the other parts. A coordinator checks every proposal against the global objective and merges proposals that do not interfere with each other. We prove linear convergence up to an error floor that vanishes when the corrections are exact. Interfering proposals can also be merged once their combination has been checked; the rate then depends on how well the proposals actually combine, not on worst-case interactions. With GPT-OSS-120B agents on robot routing, a three-agent team finds collision-free plans in every run, better than those of a single agent that controls all robots. On a larger routing task, a six-agent team completes its search about twice as fast as the single agent (in median). Merging the best checked combination of proposals, rather than only proposals that do not interfere, cuts the team's search time by about 30%. With constants measured on the runs, our convergence bound holds in every round and follows the observed progress. We also test the theory on query planning in SQLite and on a synthetic task.

infographic.key_insight: Agent collaboration admits linear convergence guarantees when local proposals account for cross-agent effects and pass a global objective check, with an error floor that vanishes under exact corrections.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a principled way to coordinate parallel AI agents while checking that merged updates improve a shared solution.
method: Model the shared solution as blocks, with each agent optimizing one block using a cross-block correction.
Globally check proposals and merge noninterfering updates.
Allow interfering updates after checking their combination; convergence rates reflect how well proposals combine.
infographic.evidence_signal: GPT-OSS-120B routing experiments report collision-free plans in every three-agent run, roughly 2× faster median search with six agents on a larger task, and about 30% less team search time using the best checked proposal combination; SQLite query planning and synthetic tasks were also tested.
infographic.watch_item: Practical gains depend on correction accuracy and the cost of globally evaluating individual proposals and their combinations.
infographic.paper_title: Local Work, Global Progress: A Convergence Theory of AI Agent Collaboration

title: SLoSa: Small, Low-Power, and Safe Foundation Models for Robotic Task Planning
authors: Weizhe Xu, Jialiang Fan, Essien Taylor, Zijun Wang, Russell Joseph, Fanxin Kong
abstract: Safe robotic task planning requires planners that can reliably achieve task goals while satisfying safety constraints. Classical planners search over explicit symbolic task representations and can provide formal guarantees with respect to encoded safety constraints, but require rigid input formats. Their computational cost also increases rapidly with the search space. In contrast, large language models (LLMs) offer flexible task interfaces and strong generalization capabilities, but they are large, power-hungry, and pre-trained with little robot-specific safety data and knowledge. Thus, they can be difficult to deploy locally on robotic systems with limited resources. To address these limitations, we present SLoSa, a neuro-symbolic compression and fine-tuning framework for training foundation-model-based robotic task planners with Small size, Low power demand, and Safety awareness. The framework first constructs a safety-aware dataset using classical planners, an advanced teacher LLM, and formal verifiers, followed by two training stages: supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning guided by a verification-based reward machine to enforce safety alignment. We evaluate SLoSa across four Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) domains, two household simulation environments, local edge platforms, and a desktop robotic arm. Across the PDDL tasks, verifier-guided post-training raises the success rate of compact 4B-14B planners to 70.5-76.0%, while INT4 deployment on a Jetson Orin requires 17.85-26.41 W of average power. Results in household simulators and on the physical robot further demonstrate the applicability of SLoSa across diverse robotic task settings.

infographic.key_insight: SLoSa combines symbolic verification with model compression and fine-tuning to build compact, safety-aware language-model planners for robots.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports local robotic task planning under resource constraints, with INT4 models averaging 17.85–26.41 W on Jetson Orin.
method: Build safety-aware training data using classical planners, a teacher LLM, and formal verifiers.
Apply supervised fine-tuning to compact foundation models.
Use reinforcement learning with a verification-based reward machine for safety alignment.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation spans four PDDL domains, two household simulators, edge platforms, and a robotic arm; verifier-guided post-training yields 70.5–76.0% success for 4B–14B planners on PDDL tasks.
infographic.watch_item: Safety alignment depends on the encoded constraints and verifier coverage; reported task success does not establish universal real-world safety.
infographic.paper_title: SLoSa: Small, Low-Power, and Safe Foundation Models for Robotic Task Planning

title: Training with ML-labeled Data via Stochastic First- and Zeroth-Order Optimization
authors: Maria-Eleni Sfyraki, Jun-Kun Wang
abstract: Training a machine learning (ML) model is an optimization process that typically requires a set of examples with ground-truth labels beforehand. Obtaining these ground truths usually requires laborious human effort and can be costly. The scalability of human labeling becomes a concern when there are a large number of data points that need to be labeled. To address this practical issue, we consider an optimization setting where a subset of samples has ground-truth labels, while the remaining data points were labeled by an ML predictor, which could potentially assign incorrect labels to those points. We propose both first-order and zeroth-order stochastic optimization methods for training on datasets consisting of a mix of true-labeled and ML-labeled samples. We further conduct comprehensive empirical studies from training a linear regression model to fine-tuning a large language model (LLM) to showcase the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms for training with ML-labeled data.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proposes stochastic optimization methods for training on a mix of ground-truth labels and potentially incorrect ML-generated labels.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This setting addresses the cost and scalability of human labeling when building training datasets.
method: Combine ground-truth-labeled samples with ML-labeled samples.
Develop stochastic first-order optimization methods.
Develop stochastic zeroth-order optimization methods.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports empirical studies spanning linear regression training to LLM fine-tuning, but provides no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Performance under different ML-label error rates remains a practical concern not quantified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Training with ML-labeled Data via Stochastic First- and Zeroth-Order Optimization

title: Large Deviations in Stochastic Dynamics: A Hamiltonian Perspective
authors: Lorenzo Cirigliano, William D. Piñeros, Anna Poggialini, Grant M. Rotskoff, Eric Vanden-Eijnden
abstract: These lecture notes present an introduction to large deviations in stochastic dynamical systems, adapted from a lecture series given at the Les Houches school ``Large Deviations: Theory and Applications'' in July 2024. The exposition develops the theory through a unified methodology: WKB analysis of backward Kolmogorov equations, which reveals the Hamiltonian structure underlying all large deviation principles considered here. We treat three asymptotic regimes systematically. First, the small-noise limit for stochastic differential equations and the large-volume limit for Markov jump processes, where the Large Deviation Principle emerges from the Law of Large Numbers through progressively finer characterizations of fluctuations. Second, the long-time limit combined with small noise, yielding the quasipotential formalism for metastability and transition rates in both equilibrium and nonequlibrium systems. Third, the long-time limit at finite noise, connecting to spectral methods via tilted generators and enabling reduction of multiscale systems. We survey computational approaches including minimum action methods, their geometric variants for quasipotential calculations, and neural network techniques. The Schlögl model of chemical bistability serves as a running example, illustrating both scalar and spatially extended settings. Appendices provide self-contained background on stochastic calculus and Markov jump processes.

infographic.key_insight: WKB analysis of backward Kolmogorov equations reveals a shared Hamiltonian structure for large deviations across weak-noise, large-volume, and long-time stochastic dynamics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This framework supports rare-event and transition-rate estimation in noisy dynamical systems, including bistable chemical reaction models.
method: Derive Hamiltonian descriptions using WKB asymptotics.
Analyze metastability with quasipotentials and finite-noise long-time behavior with tilted generators.
Survey minimum action methods, geometric variants, and neural network techniques.
infographic.evidence_signal: These lecture notes illustrate the theory with scalar and spatially extended Schlögl models; the abstract reports no quantitative benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The asymptotic regimes are distinct, so approximations must be matched carefully to the system’s noise level, volume, and observation timescale.
infographic.paper_title: Large Deviations in Stochastic Dynamics: A Hamiltonian Perspective

title: ReuF2F: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Formalized Undergraduate Research Problems
authors: Zeyu Zheng, Yiyang Liu, Yuyang Zhao, Congmin Zheng, Jiachen Zhu, Jianian Chen
abstract: As AI systems begin to resolve open research problems, reliable verification becomes increasingly important. Formal mathematics provides a trusted framework for mathematical reasoning, enabling agents to produce machine-checkable proofs while conducting mathematical exploration. Existing formal mathematics benchmarks often focus on known results or a small set of prominent open problems, which can become difficult to evaluate reliably once solutions are discovered and widely disseminated. Existing evaluation protocols are also not always aligned with how modern coding agents operate. We therefore introduce ReuF2F, a Lean 4 benchmark of 244 formalized open problems drawn from Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU), spanning entry-level open research problems across a broad range of mathematical subfields. We expect these less prominent open problems, which tend to attract less attention and may remain unsolved for longer, to be better suited for held-out evaluation of end-to-end open problem resolution in Lean. We adopt a standard coding-agent evaluation setting, placing each problem and its logical negation into a Lean project in a Docker container. We also build Leanimum-agent on mini-SWE-agent to provide a unified harness for fair comparisons across models. Our evaluation finds that even the best-performing model resolves only ~40% of the problems, leaving substantial room for improvement on formalized open research problems.

infographic.key_insight: ReuF2F benchmarks coding agents on formalized undergraduate-level open research problems, with the best evaluated model resolving only about 40%.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Lean 4 verification and a containerized coding-agent workflow provide a practical testbed for machine-checkable mathematical problem solving.
method: Formalize 244 REU open problems across diverse mathematical subfields in Lean 4.
Place each problem and its logical negation in a Lean project inside a Docker container.
Use Leanimum-agent, built on mini-SWE-agent, as a unified evaluation harness.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across the 244-problem benchmark, the best-performing evaluated model resolves approximately 40% of problems.
infographic.watch_item: Less prominent problems may reduce solution exposure, but their long-term suitability for held-out evaluation remains uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: ReuF2F: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Formalized Undergraduate Research Problems

title: Formalizing Cooperation and Competition: An AI-Assisted Mathematical Addendum to a 2018 Planning Thesis
authors: Haitham Masaud Amar
abstract: We present an AI-assisted mathematical addendum to Strategic Trip Planning: Striking a Balance Between Competition and Cooperation (Amar, 2018). We reconstruct selected relationships between strategic choice, cooperative stability, participant approval and enforcement. The thesis's Nash-to-core proposition is under-specified until outsider opportunities are stated. We verify two-person implications under fixed outsiders and explicit efficiency conditions. Under isolation, the original example has an empty TU core; its funded counterpart uses an explicit external subsidy. For a monotone resource model we characterize the exact financing gap. A finite negotiation procedure implemented in Lean is proved to terminate with participant approval, joint-cost non-worsening and local optimality against permitted approved moves. Supporting formalizations address bargaining geometry and regret-based efficiency. A resource-game counterinstance shows why monotonicity alone provides no uniform price-of-anarchy bound. Reproducible computations compare a documented heuristic reconstruction with the verified procedure on 44 source-based instances and 96 starting cases from four additional synthetic network families. Acceptance-matched heuristic and randomized pairwise-search controls contextualize the optimization results. The mathematical ingredients are established results; the contribution is a traceable reconstruction linking source statements, explicit assumptions, checked proofs, executable code and retained counterinstances. The study illustrates how AI-assisted investigation can turn engineering intuitions from legacy research into precise mathematical claims whose conditions and computational consequences can be inspected and reproduced.

infographic.key_insight: AI-assisted reconstruction turns legacy planning claims about cooperation and competition into explicit, formally checked guarantees while exposing missing assumptions and counterexamples.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The verified negotiation procedure guarantees termination, participant approval, joint-cost non-worsening and local optimality against permitted approved moves.
method: Specify outsider opportunities and efficiency conditions for Nash-to-core implications.
Formalize negotiation in Lean and characterize the financing gap in a monotone resource model.
Retain counterexamples and compare the verified procedure with heuristic and randomized controls.
infographic.evidence_signal: Reproducible computations cover 44 source-based instances and 96 starting cases across four additional synthetic network families, with acceptance-matched heuristic and randomized pairwise-search controls.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees depend on explicit assumptions and permitted moves; monotonicity alone provides no uniform price-of-anarchy bound.
infographic.paper_title: Formalizing Cooperation and Competition: An AI-Assisted Mathematical Addendum to a 2018 Planning Thesis

title: Norm-optimal model order reduction in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces
authors: Tamás Dózsa, Andrea Angino, Rolf Krause, Matthias Voigt
abstract: We consider the problem of model order reduction (MOR) in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs). We prove generalizations of well-known necessary interpolatory conditions for norm-optimal reduced-order models, originally stated for rational functions in $H_2$ Hardy-Hilbert spaces. We construct an alternative to the iterative rational Krylov (IRKA) algorithm for RKHSs with differentiable kernels to obtain norm-optimal reduced-order models. Then, we introduce generalized Malmquist-Takenaka (GMT) functions that can be used to define orthonormal bases in an arbitrary RKHS. Using GMT functions, we propose unitary transformations between separable RKHSs. This allows us to extend our optimality conditions and subsequent algorithms to MOR problems posed in RKHSs with non-differentiable kernels. The potential and versatility of the proposed MOR framework is demonstrated in several numerical experiments. We perform norm-optimal MOR on various machine learning models such as support vector machines and deep ReLU networks. In addition, we show how the proposed MOR framework can be used to solve seemingly unrelated problems. In particular, we provide an example for fitting high degree polynomials to data and also obtain a FEM-like method for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) with an optimal kernel basis.

infographic.key_insight: Model order reduction in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces can extend beyond classical rational models through generalized optimality conditions and kernel-based algorithms.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports norm-based reduction of machine learning models and optimized kernel representations for polynomial fitting and PDE approximation.
method: Generalize necessary interpolatory conditions for norm-optimal reduced models to RKHSs.
Construct an alternative to IRKA for differentiable kernels.
Use generalized Malmquist–Takenaka bases and unitary transformations to extend the approach to non-differentiable kernels.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments cover support vector machines, deep ReLU networks, high-degree polynomial fitting, and a FEM-like PDE method, but the abstract reports no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Necessary optimality conditions alone do not guarantee globally optimal reduced models; practical convergence and computational costs require evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: Norm-optimal model order reduction in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces
